title: Trentino-Alto Adige
description: Italy's Alpine north: fresh whites, Lagrein and the mountain sparkling wine Trentodoc.
L: Trentino-Alto Adige is Italy's northernmost wine region, in the Alps, along the Adige river valley. It has two provinces: Trentino in the south, Italian-speaking, and Alto Adige, or Südtirol, in the north, mostly German-speaking. Vineyards climb from about 200 to over 1,000 m on steep valley slopes.

The Alps block cold northern winds, so the valleys are surprisingly warm and sunny by day, with over 300 sunny days a year in Bolzano. Nights are cold, thanks to altitude and mountain air. That large day and night range gives aromatic whites with fresh acidity and ripe reds on the warm valley floors.
Why are Alto Adige's whites so fresh?
Altitude and cold air keep acidity high.

Alto Adige belonged to Austria until 1919, so German is widely spoken and many labels are bilingual, like Südtirol and Alto Adige. Co-operatives, Kellereien, make most of the wine, with high quality; Cantina Terlano is a famous one. Trentino, more Italian in culture, is known for sparkling wine.
Alto Adige was part of Austria until 1919.
Yes, which explains its German-speaking culture.

About two-thirds of production is white. Pinot Grigio, Chardonnay, Pinot Bianco, Sauvignon Blanc, Müller-Thurgau and Gewürztraminer are common. Gewürztraminer takes its name from Tramin, or Termeno, a village in Alto Adige. Alto Adige's whites are crisp, aromatic and precise.

Lagrein gives deep, dark reds with plum, chocolate and firm tannins, and a rosé called Kretzer. Schiava, or Vernatsch, gives light, pale, fruity reds, like Santa Maddalena. Teroldego, in Trentino's Rotaliano plain, gives dark, juicy reds. Marzemino is another Trentino red. Pinot Noir, called Blauburgunder, is increasingly serious.

Schiava is one of the few red wines that's great lightly chilled. Its low tannin and fresh fruit suit summer.

Trentodoc, created in 1993, was one of the first Italian DOCs for traditional method sparkling wine. It's made mainly from Chardonnay, with Pinot Noir, Pinot Bianco and Pinot Meunier, grown in Trentino's mountain vineyards, often at 300 to 800 m. Altitude gives high acidity, ideal for sparkling wine.

Trentodoc must be made by the traditional method, with second fermentation in bottle. Minimum lees ageing: 15 months for non-vintage, 24 months for vintage, 36 months for Riserva. The styles range from Pas Dosé to Demi-Sec. The wines are crisp, fine and elegant, often compared with Champagne.

Giulio Ferrari founded his sparkling wine house in Trento in 1902, after studying in Champagne, and brought Chardonnay to the region. Ferrari, owned since 1952 by the Lunelli family, remains Trentodoc's leading producer. Its Giulio Ferrari Riserva del Fondatore is one of Italy's most acclaimed sparkling wines.

Alto Adige labels are often bilingual: Alto Adige or Südtirol, Pinot Grigio or Ruländer, Lagrein or Lagrein Dunkel. Most wines are varietal, named by grape. Trentino labels name the grape or Trentodoc. Kellerei or Cantina means a winery, often a co-operative.

The region's food blends Italian and Austrian: speck, smoked ham; canederli, bread dumplings; strudel; polenta; and mountain cheeses. Pinot Bianco and Pinot Grigio suit speck and light dishes; Gewürztraminer suits spicy food and cheese; Lagrein suits game, goulash and grilled meat; Trentodoc suits aperitifs and fried food.
